title: A waiting list for things you want
description: Write down what you want instead of buying it, date it, and revisit it in a month. Most wants quietly expire; the survivors are worth your money.

body.heading: Catch the want, keep the money
paragraphs: When you feel the pull to buy something non-essential, add it to a waiting list instead of a basket: the item, the price, and today's date. Then close the shop tab. You have honoured the desire without spending anything.

This works because wanting is often about the moment — the image, the novelty, the mood. Written down, the want gets a fair hearing later, when the moment has passed and your judgement is back on duty.

body.heading: The thirty-day review
paragraphs: Once a month, read the list. Cross off everything that makes you shrug. What remains — the thing you still genuinely want after thirty days — has earned consideration, ideally from a treats pot you have been feeding.
You will find most entries expire on their own. That is not deprivation; that is discovering how many purchases were only ever weather.

body.heading: A kinder way to say no
paragraphs: The list never says never; it says "not yet, and let us check." That makes it far easier to keep than a blunt ban — and bans are famous for ending in splurges.

Keep the list somewhere you will actually see it — a note on your phone beats a notebook in a drawer. Reviewing it should feel like browsing your own past wishes, half amusement and half relief at the money still in your account.

takeaway: Park every non-essential want on a dated list for thirty days. Most will fade; the few that survive deserve a planned place in your budget.
